title: Button Night Light
intro: Press a button to turn a light on and off. Then make it remember what it was doing.

wiring_steps.title: The LED
wiring_steps.text: Unplug the USB cable before you change any wires. Plug it back in when you're done. Start with the power rails: a black wire from GND on your board to the blue (−) rail at the bottom of the breadboard, and a red wire from {{VCC}} to the red (+) rail. Push the LED into holes H5 and H6, with the long leg (+) in H6. Put a 220Ω resistor from G5 across the gap to E5. Add a wire from {{pin:LED_PIN}} to J6, and a black wire from A5 to the blue (−) rail at the bottom.

wiring_steps.title: The button
wiring_steps.text: Press the button into the middle of the breadboard so it sits across the gap: its legs go in F14, F16, E14 and E16. Add a wire from {{pin:BUTTON_PIN}} to J14, and a black wire from A16 to the blue (−) rail. (The code turns on the pin's pull-up, so no resistor is needed.)

steps.title: Test the LED
steps.text:
One part at a time! First let's check the LED works on its own: turn it on and leave it on.

**Your task:** fill in the blank so the LED turns on, then press **Run**.
hints: Use `HIGH` to turn the LED on.

checks.label: I saw the LED light up

steps.success: The LED works. Now let's check the button.

steps.title: Read the button
steps.text:
`digitalRead(BUTTON_PIN)` asks: is the button's pin HIGH (1) or LOW (0)?

With `INPUT_PULLUP`, the board gently pulls the pin up to HIGH. Pressing the button connects it to GND, so a **pressed button reads 0** and a released one reads **1**. It seems backwards, but it saves a resistor!

**Your task:** Run this code, open the **Serial Monitor**, and press the button. Watch the numbers change.
hints: In the simulator, click and hold the button on the breadboard.
The Serial Monitor is under the code. 1 means not pressed, 0 means pressed.
Hold the button down for a moment so you see a few 0s.

checks.label: I saw 0 when I pressed the button

steps.success: The board can feel the button! Reading inputs like this is how every game controller and keyboard works.

steps.title: Button controls the light
steps.text:
Now join the two parts: when the button is pressed, the light comes on.

An `if` asks a question. `==` means "is it equal to?" (two equals signs: one `=` would change the value instead).

**Your task:** fill in the blanks so the LED is on while the button is held down.
hints: A pressed button reads `LOW` (remember the 0 in the Serial Monitor?).
The first blank is `LOW`. What turns the LED off?

checks.label: The light comes on when you press
The light goes off when you let go
The light is on only while I hold the button

steps.success: Your code decides what to do. That's an algorithm with a decision in it.

steps.title: Remember on and off
steps.text:
**Goal:** press once and the light stays on. Press again and it turns off.

Your code needs to remember whether the light is on (a `bool` variable), and to notice the moment the button goes *down*, not the whole time it's held.
hints: Make a variable above `setup()`: `bool lightOn = false;`. `lightOn = !lightOn;` flips it.
Remember the button's last reading in another variable. A new press is when it was `HIGH` last time and is `LOW` now.
Look at the goal with **Watch the goal**, then compare it with your code line by line.

checks.label: The first press turns the light on
The next press turns it off

steps.success: Your night light remembers! Keeping track of what's going on is called keeping state.

outro: Your night light listens to a button and remembers what it's doing. You used **digitalRead**, **if / else** and a **variable** to remember the light's state.
stretch: Make the light turn itself off 10 seconds after it was turned on. (Use `millis()`.)
Make a long press do something different from a short press.
Count how many times the button has been pressed and print it to the Serial Monitor.
